Why Own a Hyperbaric Chamber at Home?

For individuals and families committed to consistent hyperbaric oxygen therapy, owning a home hyperbaric chamber offers significant advantages over visiting a clinic. Home ownership eliminates the need to schedule appointments, travel to a facility, and wait for available session times. Instead, you can incorporate HBOT into your daily routine on your own schedule, making it far easier to maintain the consistency that is important for building on the cumulative effects of repeated sessions.

A home hyperbaric chamber also serves as a shared wellness resource for the entire household. The Science

How Home Hyperbaric Chambers Work

Home hyperbaric chambers deliver mild hyperbaric oxygen therapy (mHBOT) at 1.3 atmospheres absolute (ATA). Based on Henry's Law of physics, this elevated pressure causes significantly more oxygen to dissolve into blood plasma than is possible under normal atmospheric conditions.

Setting up a home hyperbaric chamber is straightforward. OxyHealth portable chambers inflate using a compact, purpose-built compressor that plugs into a standard household electrical outlet. No special wiring, dedicated circuits, or professional installation is required. An oxygen concentrator connects to the chamber to deliver concentrated oxygen during the session. Once inflated, you simply enter the chamber, seal the zipper closure, and relax while the compressor maintains the therapeutic pressure of 1.3 ATA throughout the session.

A typical session lasts between 60 and 90 minutes. During this time, many users read, watch content on a tablet or phone, listen to music or podcasts, meditate, or simply rest. The chamber features transparent viewing panels that allow natural light in and reduce any feeling of confinement. After the session, the chamber can remain inflated for the next use or be deflated and stored compactly when not needed. The entire system is designed to integrate seamlessly into your daily life at home.

Understanding Portable HBOT

What Is a Portable Hyperbaric Chamber?

A portable hyperbaric chamber is a soft-shell, inflatable pressurized enclosure that delivers mild hyperbaric oxygen therapy (mHBOT) at 1.3 atmospheres absolute (ATA). These chambers are constructed from medical-grade materials and are designed to be set up and operated in any standard room with a household electrical outlet. Unlike fixed clinical hard-shell chambers that require permanent installation in a medical facility, portable chambers can be assembled in minutes and moved between locations as needed.

The fundamental difference between portable and fixed clinical chambers lies in construction and pressure capability. Portable chambers use a soft-shell, inflatable design that reaches 1.3 ATA (approximately 4 psi above normal atmospheric pressure), while clinical hard-shell chambers are built from rigid steel and can operate at pressures up to 4.0 ATA. Both types increase oxygen dissolution into blood plasma based on Henry's Law of physics, but they serve different use cases. Portable chambers are suited for home wellness protocols, clinic treatment rooms, and mobile applications, while clinical chambers are designed for hospital settings and FDA-cleared medical conditions that may require higher pressures.

OxyHealth has manufactured portable hyperbaric chambers since 1997, with over 19,000 chambers delivered worldwide. Every OxyHealth portable chamber is FDA 510(k) cleared and built to ASME PVHO-1 pressure vessel standards, setting the benchmark for safety and quality in the portable HBOT category.

The Science

How Portable Hyperbaric Chambers Work

Portable hyperbaric chambers work by creating a pressurized environment at 1.3 ATA using a purpose-built air compressor. When the chamber is sealed and the compressor is activated, air is pumped into the soft-shell enclosure until the internal pressure reaches 1.3 atmospheres absolute, which is approximately 4 pounds per square inch above normal atmospheric pressure. At this elevated pressure, oxygen molecules decrease in size and dissolve more readily into blood plasma, increasing total oxygen delivery throughout the body.

The inflatable design of a portable chamber is engineered from medical-grade materials that maintain structural integrity under pressure. Each OxyHealth portable chamber includes a dedicated compressor that has been specifically designed for that model, ensuring consistent pressurization and quiet operation. Users can enhance their sessions by pairing the chamber with an oxygen concentrator, which delivers concentrated oxygen (typically 90-95% purity) through a mask or cannula while inside the pressurized environment.

A typical session in a portable hyperbaric chamber lasts 60 to 90 minutes. The pressurization cycle takes a few minutes at the start, followed by the treatment period at full pressure, and a gradual depressurization at the end. Many users read, watch videos, or rest comfortably during their sessions. The chamber operates on a standard household electrical outlet, requiring no special wiring or infrastructure modifications.

The Fundamentals

What is Mild Hyperbaric Therapy?

Mild hyperbaric oxygen therapy, commonly referred to as mHBOT, is a form of hyperbaric oxygen therapy that operates at 1.3 ATA (atmospheres absolute). This represents a pressure roughly 30% above normal sea-level atmospheric pressure. During a mild hyperbaric session, the user enters a portable, soft-shell chamber and breathes concentrated oxygen while the chamber is pressurized to 1.3 ATA. The combination of elevated pressure and supplemental oxygen allows more oxygen to dissolve into blood plasma than is possible under normal conditions.

Unlike higher-pressure clinical HBOT, which is administered in rigid monoplace or multiplace chambers at medical facilities and can reach pressures of 2.0 to 3.0 ATA, mild hyperbaric therapy is designed for accessibility and comfort. The portable chambers used for mHBOT are lightweight, can be set up in a home or office, and do not require the specialized infrastructure associated with hospital-grade hyperbaric systems. This makes mild hyperbaric therapy an option for individuals seeking to incorporate oxygen therapy into their daily wellness routine without traveling to a clinical facility.

The Science

How 1.3 ATA Therapy Works

The science behind mild hyperbaric therapy is grounded in Henry's Law, a principle of physics stating that the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid. In practical terms, when the atmospheric pressure inside a hyperbaric chamber is increased to 1.3 ATA, the elevated pressure causes more oxygen to dissolve into the blood plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, and other body fluids beyond what hemoglobin alone can carry.

Under normal sea-level conditions (1.0 ATA), oxygen transport relies almost entirely on hemoglobin molecules in red blood cells. Hemoglobin is typically saturated at around 97% under normal conditions, leaving very little room for additional oxygen to be carried by this pathway. However, when pressure is increased, oxygen dissolves directly into the plasma itself. This dissolved oxygen is not bound to hemoglobin and can therefore reach tissues and areas of the body that may have restricted blood flow or compromised capillary networks.

At 1.3 ATA, the pressure increase is gentle enough that most users find the experience comfortable and easy to tolerate. The sensation is similar to the pressure change experienced during a short airplane descent. Users typically equalize ear pressure by swallowing or gently popping their ears, and within minutes the chamber reaches its target pressure. Sessions generally last 60 to 90 minutes, during which users can read, watch content on a device, meditate, or simply rest.

The accessibility of 1.3 ATA therapy is one of its defining features. Because the pressure is relatively low, the chambers can be constructed from flexible, durable materials rather than the rigid steel or acrylic required for higher-pressure clinical systems. This allows mild hyperbaric chambers to be portable, lightweight, and suitable for residential environments without structural modifications to the home.

This is a formal regulatory pathway where the manufacturer submits detailed evidence demonstrating that the device is safe and effective for its intended use. The FDA reviews this submission, evaluates the data, and issues a clearance letter only when the device meets the agency's safety and performance standards.

Hyperbaric chambers are classified by the FDA as Class II medical devices. Class II devices are considered moderate risk and require regulatory controls beyond the general controls applied to Class I devices. The 510(k) pathway requires the manufacturer to demonstrate that the device is "substantially equivalent" to a legally marketed predicate device. This means the chamber must perform at least as safely and effectively as devices already on the market.

The 510(k) submission typically includes data on biocompatibility testing, electrical safety testing, pressure system integrity, material safety, labeling review, and overall device performance. The FDA may request additional information or testing before issuing clearance. This process can take several months and represents a significant investment by the manufacturer in demonstrating product safety.

Once a device receives 510(k) clearance, the manufacturer is assigned a clearance number (formatted as K followed by six digits) and may legally market the device in the United States. The clearance is specific to the device as described in the submission, and any significant changes to the device's design, materials, or intended use may require a new 510(k) submission.

Buyer Checklist

What to Ask Before Buying Any Chamber

Before purchasing a hyperbaric chamber from any manufacturer, use this checklist to verify safety, quality, and credibility. Do not rely solely on marketing materials or website claims.

Can they provide the FDA 510(k) clearance letter?

Ask for the 510(k) clearance number (K-number) and verify it in the FDA database at accessdata.fda.gov. If the manufacturer can only provide an FDA registration number or establishment listing, that is not 510(k) clearance and does not demonstrate that the device has been reviewed for safety.

Can they provide the ASME PVHO-1 GR-1 form?

The GR-1 form is the official ASME documentation that confirms a pressure vessel has been designed, fabricated, and tested to PVHO-1 standards. If a manufacturer claims ASME compliance but cannot produce this form, the claim is not verified.

Can they show the ISO 13485 certificate?

ISO 13485 certification is issued by accredited third-party auditors. Ask for a copy of the certificate and verify that it is current, as ISO certifications require regular renewal through re-audits. Check that the scope of the certificate covers hyperbaric chamber manufacturing.

Are the electrical components UL listed?

UL listing can be verified through the UL product database. Ask the manufacturer for their UL file number and confirm that the listing covers the electrical components used in the chamber. This is particularly important for hyperbaric chambers because they operate in oxygen-enriched environments.

What does the warranty cover, and for how long?

Understand exactly what is covered by the warranty, including the chamber itself, the compressor system, and any accessories. Ask about the process for filing a warranty claim and the typical turnaround time for repairs or replacements.

Where is customer support located?

Knowing where the manufacturer customer support team is based matters for responsiveness and communication. Ask whether support is available by phone, how quickly they respond to inquiries, and whether they can dispatch service technicians if needed.

Regulatory Guide

Do You Need a Prescription for a Hyperbaric Chamber?

Yes. Hyperbaric chambers are FDA-regulated Class II medical devices, and OxyHealth chambers are sold on the order of a licensed healthcare provider, for home use and clinic use alike. The prescription is part of how the device is regulated. It is not a formality.

Why a prescription is required

A hyperbaric chamber raises the pressure around the whole body above normal atmospheric pressure. That makes it a medical device. FDA lists hyperbaric chambers under Product Code CBF and regulation 21 CFR 868.5470 as Class II devices that go through 510(k) premarket review.

FDA 510(k) clearance concerns the device itself: its design, performance, labeling, and manufacturing controls. The prescription requirement sits alongside that clearance. It makes sure a licensed healthcare provider is involved before a person begins using a pressurized device.

Calling a chamber a wellness product does not change this

Some sellers describe full-body chambers as wellness or lifestyle products. A marketing label does not change how FDA classifies a hyperbaric chamber. If you are comparing sellers, ask for the device's 510(k) clearance and confirm it in FDA's device classification database, and ask how the seller handles the prescription requirement.

What the prescription covers, and what it does not

A prescription authorizes a person to obtain and use the device under a clinician's direction. The clinician, not the manufacturer, determines:

  • Whether hyperbaric therapy is appropriate for the individual
  • The breathing gas and any supplemental oxygen
  • The pressure, stated in ATA
  • Session length, frequency, and total number of sessions

These variables together make up the dose. Pressure and oxygen concentration are separate variables, and two protocols that share a name can deliver very different exposures. OxyHealth does not prescribe protocols or recommend session counts.

Device clearance and clinical use are different things

FDA clearance applies to a device and its cleared labeling. How a physician uses a cleared device for a particular patient is a separate medical judgment. Research on conditions outside a device's cleared indications does not mean the device is cleared for those uses, and a physician's decision to use a cleared device does not make the device uncleared.

How the process works with OxyHealth

  1. Speak with a licensed healthcare provider about whether hyperbaric therapy is appropriate for you.
  2. Contact OxyHealth to discuss chamber types and what documentation is needed.
  3. Your provider supplies the prescription and determines your protocol.
  4. Follow the chamber's instructions for use and the training OxyHealth provides.

A prescription does not determine insurance coverage. See the insurance coverage guide for how payers approach hyperbaric therapy.

The Science

How Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy Works

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) involves breathing concentrated oxygen inside a pressurized chamber. Based on Henry's Law of physics, increasing the atmospheric pressure around the body causes significantly more oxygen to dissolve directly into blood plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, and other body fluids. This dissolved oxygen can reach tissues and areas of the body that red blood cells may not easily access, particularly in regions with compromised blood flow.

Under normal conditions, oxygen is carried almost exclusively by hemoglobin in red blood cells. In a hyperbaric environment, the elevated pressure forces oxygen to dissolve into plasma at levels far beyond what is possible at sea level. This oxygen-rich plasma can penetrate damaged, swollen, or poorly vascularized tissues, delivering the oxygen needed to support cellular repair and metabolic processes.

OxyHealth chambers are available in both portable models for home use (operating at 1.3 ATA) and clinical models for medical facilities (capable of higher pressures). All OxyHealth chambers are FDA-cleared and manufactured under strict quality controls to ensure safety and effectiveness.

Reduced Inflammation

Research suggests that HBOT may help modulate the inflammatory response by reducing levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6. Studies have shown that pressurized oxygen can help downregulate inflammatory pathways, potentially supporting recovery from both acute and chronic inflammatory conditions.

Improved Athletic Recovery

A study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine (Staples et al., 1999) found that athletes using HBOT experienced faster recovery from ankle sprains compared to a control group. Many professional athletes use HBOT to support recovery from training and competition.

Anti-Aging and Longevity

A landmark study from Tel Aviv University (Hachmo et al., 2020, published in the journal Aging) found that HBOT increased telomere length by over 20% and reduced senescent cell populations by up to 37% in aging adults. These biological markers are closely associated with cellular aging.

Enhanced Cognitive Function

Research suggests that HBOT may improve cerebral blood flow and support neuroplasticity. Studies published in journals such as Frontiers in Human Neuroscience have explored how increased oxygen delivery to the brain may support cognitive performance, memory, and recovery from neurological conditions.

Increased Stem Cell Mobilization

Research has shown that HBOT may stimulate the release of stem cells from bone marrow into the bloodstream, with studies reporting up to an 800% increase in circulating stem cells after a series of treatments. These stem cells play a key role in tissue repair and regeneration throughout the body.

Safety Profile

Is Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy Safe?

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) has been used safely for decades across medical, clinical, and wellness settings. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has cleared HBOT for 14 specific medical conditions, and it is administered routinely in hospitals, wound care centers, and home environments around the world. When used in FDA-cleared chambers and following established protocols, HBOT is considered safe and well-tolerated by the vast majority of users.

OxyHealth, a hyperbaric chamber manufacturer since 1997, has delivered over 19,000 chambers worldwide and maintains an exceptional safety record spanning more than 29 years. Every OxyHealth chamber is FDA 510(k)-cleared, built to ASME PVHO-1 pressure vessel standards, manufactured under ISO 13485 quality management certification, and features UL-listed electrical components. More than 3,000 physicians trust OxyHealth technology in their practices.

Like any medical device or therapy, HBOT may produce some side effects, though these are generally mild and temporary. Understanding what to expect before your first session helps you prepare and communicate effectively with your healthcare provider or chamber operator. The sections below provide a comprehensive overview of possible side effects, organized by how frequently they occur.

It is always important to consult with a qualified healthcare provider before starting any hyperbaric oxygen therapy protocol. Your physician can evaluate your individual health history, current medications, and any conditions that may require special consideration.

Generally Mild and Temporary

Common Side Effects

The following side effects are the most frequently reported. They are considered mild, typically resolve on their own shortly after a session, and often diminish with subsequent sessions as the body acclimates.

Ear Pressure and Barotrauma

The most commonly reported side effect is a sensation of pressure or fullness in the ears during the pressurization and depressurization phases. This is similar to what many people experience during air travel or scuba diving. The middle ear must equalize to match the changing pressure inside the chamber. Simple techniques such as yawning, swallowing, or the Valsalva maneuver (gently blowing with your nose pinched) can relieve this sensation. If equalization is difficult, the operator can slow the rate of pressurization to allow more time for adjustment.

Temporary Fatigue

Some people feel mildly tired or relaxed after an HBOT session. This is a common response and may be related to the body processing increased oxygen levels. The fatigue is generally short-lived and many users report feeling re-energized within a few hours. Staying hydrated before and after your session and allowing time to rest afterward can help manage this effect.

Mild Lightheadedness

A brief period of lightheadedness or dizziness may occur during or immediately after a session, particularly for first-time users. This is typically related to the change in atmospheric pressure and increased oxygen concentration. The sensation usually passes quickly after returning to normal atmospheric pressure. Moving slowly when exiting the chamber and sitting for a moment before standing can help.

Sinus Pressure

Similar to ear pressure, the sinuses may feel congested or pressurized during a session, especially during changes in pressure. People with pre-existing sinus congestion or a mild cold may notice this more. Ensuring your sinuses are relatively clear before a session and using decongestant spray if recommended by your physician can help minimize discomfort. If sinus pressure is persistent, discuss it with your healthcare provider.

Infrequent

Less Common Side Effects

The following side effects are reported less frequently. When they do occur, they are typically temporary and resolve after the treatment course is completed.

Temporary Vision Changes

Some individuals who undergo multiple HBOT sessions may experience a temporary shift in vision, most commonly a mild increase in nearsightedness (myopia). This is believed to be related to changes in the lens of the eye caused by prolonged exposure to elevated oxygen levels. The effect is generally reversible, and vision typically returns to its pre-treatment baseline within several weeks after completing a course of sessions.

This effect is more commonly associated with higher-pressure clinical protocols (above 1.5 ATA) conducted over many sessions. Users of mild portable chambers operating at 1.3 ATA are less likely to experience this effect. If you notice any changes in vision during a treatment course, inform your healthcare provider.

Claustrophobia

Some individuals may feel anxious or uncomfortable in the enclosed space of a hyperbaric chamber, especially during their first session. This is not a physiological side effect of the therapy itself but rather a response to the enclosed environment. The degree of discomfort varies from person to person and is influenced by chamber design and individual sensitivity.

OxyHealth designs its chambers with spacious interiors, clear viewing panels, and internal communication systems specifically to minimize feelings of confinement. The Vitaeris 320, for example, features transparent walls that allow natural light and a full view of the surroundings. Many users who feel apprehensive during their first session become comfortable within just one or two sessions. Operators can also adjust the pace of pressurization to help new users acclimate gradually.

Very Rare

Rare Side Effects

The following side effects are extremely rare and are primarily associated with high-pressure clinical protocols rather than mild portable chamber use. They are included here for completeness and transparency.

Oxygen Toxicity

Oxygen toxicity can occur when the body is exposed to very high concentrations of oxygen at elevated pressures for extended periods. It most commonly affects the central nervous system or the lungs. Symptoms may include nausea, muscle twitching, or breathing discomfort.

This risk is primarily associated with pressures above 2.0 ATA with pure oxygen delivery over prolonged sessions. OxyHealth portable chambers operate at 1.3 ATA with ambient air, which is well within safe parameters. Clinical protocols at higher pressures include strict time limits and monitoring to prevent oxygen toxicity. Proper adherence to prescribed session durations and pressures makes this an extremely unlikely occurrence.

Seizure

Seizures related to HBOT are extremely rare and are associated with oxygen toxicity at high pressures, typically above 2.0 ATA with pure oxygen. The incidence in clinical settings is reported to be very low. These events are typically brief and self-limiting, resolving once the oxygen exposure is reduced.

At the mild pressures used in portable hyperbaric chambers (1.3 ATA), this risk is considered negligible. Clinical facilities that operate at higher pressures follow established safety protocols, including continuous monitoring and prescribed session durations, to mitigate this risk. Individuals with a history of seizure disorders should discuss HBOT with their physician before beginning treatment.

Important Safety Information

Who Should Not Use HBOT

While hyperbaric oxygen therapy is safe for most people, there are certain conditions and circumstances where HBOT may not be appropriate. It is essential to provide your healthcare provider with a complete medical history before beginning any hyperbaric therapy protocol. The following are recognized contraindications and precautions.

Absolute Contraindications

  • Untreated Pneumothorax: A collapsed lung that has not been treated is the primary absolute contraindication for HBOT. The pressure changes inside the chamber could worsen this condition.

Relative Contraindications

  • Certain Medications: Some medications, including certain chemotherapy agents, may interact with elevated oxygen levels. Consult your physician if you are taking any prescription medications.
  • Specific Lung Conditions: Conditions such as emphysema with air trapping or a history of spontaneous pneumothorax may increase risk during pressurization. Medical evaluation is recommended.
  • Upper Respiratory Infections: Active sinus or upper respiratory infections may make equalization difficult and increase discomfort during pressure changes.
  • Pregnancy: The effects of HBOT during pregnancy have not been extensively studied. Pregnant individuals should consult their physician before considering hyperbaric therapy.

Always consult your physician. This page is intended for informational purposes only and does not replace professional medical advice. A qualified healthcare provider can evaluate your complete medical history and determine whether HBOT is appropriate for your individual situation.

Equalize Your Ears

Practice equalization techniques before your session. Yawning, swallowing, or gently blowing with your nose pinched (the Valsalva maneuver) can help relieve ear pressure during pressurization. Let your operator know if you have difficulty equalizing so they can adjust the rate.

Stay Hydrated

Whether insurance covers hyperbaric oxygen therapy depends on several factors, including the medical condition being treated, the type of insurance plan, and the specific insurer's policies. In general, HBOT is most likely to be covered when it is prescribed for one of the 14 conditions that the FDA has cleared for hyperbaric treatment and when a physician documents medical necessity.

Medicare, Medicaid, and many private insurance plans provide coverage for HBOT when used to treat FDA-cleared indications. Coverage typically requires a physician's prescription, a documented diagnosis, and in many cases, pre-authorization from the insurance provider. The scope of coverage, including the number of sessions approved and the reimbursement rate, varies between plans and providers.

For off-label uses of HBOT, such as wellness, athletic recovery, or anti-aging protocols, insurance coverage is generally not available. However, the growing body of research supporting HBOT for various conditions means that coverage policies continue to evolve. It is always worth checking with your specific insurance provider for the most current coverage details related to your condition and treatment plan.

Federal Coverage

Medicare Coverage for Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy

Medicare Part B covers hyperbaric oxygen therapy for 14 Medicare-covered conditions. Coverage requires that the treatment be ordered by a physician and performed in an approved facility using an FDA-cleared hyperbaric chamber. Below are the 14 conditions for which Medicare provides HBOT coverage.

Air or Gas Embolism

Treatment for air or gas bubbles in the bloodstream, which can occur during surgical procedures or diving accidents.

Carbon Monoxide Poisoning

HBOT accelerates the removal of carbon monoxide from the bloodstream by replacing it with oxygen under pressure.

Gas Gangrene (Clostridial Myonecrosis)

A serious bacterial infection of muscle tissue where elevated oxygen levels help inhibit the growth of anaerobic bacteria.

Crush Injuries and Acute Traumatic Ischemias

HBOT supports oxygen delivery to tissue compromised by crushing force, helping reduce swelling and support tissue viability.

Decompression Sickness

The primary treatment for "the bends" experienced by divers, where HBOT helps dissolve nitrogen bubbles in the blood.

Arterial Insufficiency (Central Retinal Artery Occlusion)

Used to improve oxygen supply in cases of acute peripheral arterial insufficiency and certain types of sudden vision loss.

Severe Anemia (Exceptional Blood Loss)

When blood transfusion is not an option, HBOT provides oxygen delivery through dissolved plasma oxygen rather than hemoglobin.

Intracranial Abscess

HBOT supports treatment of brain abscesses by enhancing oxygen delivery to the infected area and supporting immune response.

Necrotizing Soft Tissue Infections

Used as adjunctive therapy for serious soft tissue infections, where elevated oxygen helps inhibit bacterial growth and supports healing.

Osteomyelitis (Refractory)

For chronic bone infections that have not responded to standard treatment, HBOT supports antibiotic effectiveness and bone healing.

Delayed Radiation Injury

HBOT helps promote new blood vessel growth in tissue damaged by radiation therapy, restoring blood flow to irradiated areas.

Compromised Skin Grafts and Flaps

When skin grafts or surgical flaps show signs of failure, HBOT supports tissue oxygenation to improve graft survival.

Acute Thermal Burn Injury

HBOT supports treatment of severe burns by reducing swelling, supporting tissue oxygenation, and helping prevent infection.

Diabetic Foot Ulcers (Wagner Grade III or Higher)

One of the most common Medicare-covered HBOT indications, used for non-healing diabetic foot wounds that have not responded to standard wound care.

Medicare coverage may also extend to Medicaid recipients in many states. Coverage specifics, including the number of approved sessions, vary by region and individual circumstances. Always verify coverage with your Medicare representative or healthcare provider before starting treatment.

Step-by-Step

How to Get Insurance Approval for HBOT

Securing insurance coverage for hyperbaric oxygen therapy involves several key steps. Following this process carefully can significantly improve your chances of getting HBOT approved and covered by your insurance plan.

Step 1

Get a Physician Prescription

The first step is to obtain a written prescription for HBOT from a licensed physician. The prescription should include your specific diagnosis, the clinical rationale for hyperbaric therapy, and the recommended treatment protocol, including the number of sessions and pressure level. A diagnosis that falls within the 14 FDA-cleared conditions significantly increases the likelihood of insurance approval.

Step 2

Obtain Pre-Authorization

Contact your insurance provider to request pre-authorization for HBOT. Most insurers require prior approval before treatment begins. During this process, you will typically need to provide your physician's prescription, your diagnosis code (ICD-10), and any supporting medical documentation. Your physician's office or the hyperbaric facility may assist with this step, as they are often experienced in working with insurance companies.

Step 3

Document Medical Necessity

Insurance companies require documentation showing that HBOT is medically necessary for your condition. This typically includes medical records showing previous treatment attempts, diagnostic imaging or wound measurements, lab results, and a detailed letter of medical necessity from your physician. The stronger the documentation, the more likely your claim is to be approved. Include any relevant peer-reviewed literature that supports HBOT for your specific condition.

Step 4

Submit Claims and Follow Up

After your pre-authorization is approved and treatment begins, ensure that claims are submitted correctly with the appropriate CPT codes for hyperbaric therapy. The treating facility will typically handle claim submission, but it is wise to track each claim and verify that your insurer is processing payments as expected. If a claim is denied, request a detailed explanation and work with your physician to submit an appeal with additional supporting documentation.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is being studied for its potential to support anti-aging and longevity by targeting fundamental biological mechanisms of cellular aging. Telomeres are the protective caps at the ends of chromosomes that shorten each time a cell divides. When telomeres become critically short, cells enter a state of senescence, where they stop dividing but remain metabolically active, releasing inflammatory signals that damage surrounding healthy tissue. This accumulation of senescent cells is a primary driver of age-related decline, contributing to reduced organ function, chronic inflammation, and increased disease susceptibility.

Researchers believe HBOT may address these aging pathways through the intermittent hyperoxia-hypoxia effect. The repeated exposure to high-pressure oxygen followed by return to normal conditions may trigger regenerative gene expression, stimulate stem cell production, support mitochondrial function, and activate the body's natural repair mechanisms. These findings have positioned HBOT as an area of active investigation in longevity science, though more research is needed to establish long-term outcomes.

The Science

How HBOT Supports Brain Health

The brain is one of the most oxygen-dependent organs in the human body, consuming approximately 20% of the body's total oxygen supply despite accounting for only about 2% of body weight. When brain tissue is injured or blood flow is compromised, the resulting oxygen deficit can impair neural function, slow recovery, and contribute to cognitive difficulties. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) addresses this by dramatically increasing the amount of dissolved oxygen in blood plasma, allowing oxygen to reach brain regions that may be underserved by normal circulation.

Under the elevated pressure of a hyperbaric chamber, oxygen dissolves into plasma at levels far exceeding what is possible at normal atmospheric pressure. This oxygen-rich plasma can penetrate areas of the brain with compromised blood flow, supporting cellular metabolism and energy production in neural tissue. Research suggests that this process may help stimulate neuroplasticity, the brain's ability to form new neural connections and reorganize existing pathways, which is fundamental to recovery from brain injuries and to maintaining cognitive function throughout aging.

A landmark series of studies from Tel Aviv University, led by Professor Shai Efrati and colleagues, has demonstrated that HBOT may significantly improve cerebral blood flow and cognitive performance in aging adults. In a randomized controlled trial (Hadanny et al., 2020, published in the journal Aging), healthy adults over 64 years of age who completed a protocol of 60 HBOT sessions showed significant improvements in attention, information processing speed, and executive function compared to a control group. Brain imaging revealed increased cerebral blood flow in regions associated with cognitive decline.

These studies reflect growing interest in understanding whether increased oxygen delivery under pressure can support neural recovery in individuals whose brain injuries have not fully responded to standard rehabilitation approaches.

Research suggests that the elevated oxygen levels achieved during HBOT sessions may help reduce neuroinflammation, a key factor in persistent concussion symptoms. The increased oxygen supply may also support the repair of microstructural damage to white matter tracts that can occur during concussive impacts, potentially facilitating improved neural signaling and cognitive function.

Understanding Inflammation

How HBOT Reduces Chronic Inflammation

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is being studied for its potential to reduce chronic inflammation by delivering concentrated oxygen under pressure to damaged and inflamed tissue. Chronic inflammation is increasingly recognized as a root factor in many of the most common health conditions, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, autoimmune disorders, neurodegenerative conditions, and chronic pain syndromes. Unlike acute inflammation, which is a healthy short-term response to injury, chronic inflammation persists for weeks, months, or years, silently damaging tissue and contributing to disease progression. Standard anti-inflammatory medications can help manage symptoms but often carry side effects with long-term use.

HBOT offers a non-pharmacological approach that is being studied for inflammation management. By increasing the partial pressure of oxygen in tissue, HBOT provides the oxygen substrate necessary for cellular repair while potentially modulating immune cell behavior. The Science

Cytokine Modulation

Research suggests HBOT may reduce the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-alpha, interleukin-1, and interleukin-6, which are key drivers of chronic inflammation. Studies also indicate it may upregulate anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10, potentially shifting the body away from a pro-inflammatory state.

Edema Reduction

Hyperbaric oxygen causes vasoconstriction in inflamed tissue, which reduces swelling and edema without compromising oxygen delivery. This is because the dissolved oxygen in plasma more than compensates for the reduced blood flow, resulting in less swelling with more oxygen reaching the affected area.

Immune Modulation

Research suggests HBOT may help regulate neutrophil adhesion and activity, potentially reducing excessive immune cell infiltration that perpetuates chronic inflammation. This proposed immune-modulatory effect may help support balanced immune function without broadly suppressing the immune system.

Tissue Repair

Oxygen is essential for every phase of tissue repair, from initial debris clearance to collagen formation and tissue remodeling. HBOT delivers increased oxygen to inflamed and damaged tissue, which may support proper healing and help address the cycle of ongoing damage and inflammation.

Oxidative Stress Balance

Research suggests that through repeated exposure to hyperbaric oxygen, HBOT may upregulate the body's endogenous antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase and glutathione. This potentially enhanced antioxidant capacity may help counteract the oxidative damage associated with chronic inflammation.

New Blood Vessel Growth

Research suggests HBOT may stimulate angiogenesis in tissue with compromised blood supply. New blood vessels may improve long-term oxygen and nutrient delivery to previously inflamed areas, potentially supporting sustained healing.

The Condition

Understanding Long COVID

Long COVID, clinically referred to as post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC), is a complex condition in which symptoms persist for weeks, months, or even years after the initial COVID-19 infection has resolved. The condition can affect individuals regardless of how mild or severe their acute illness was, and it has emerged as a significant public health challenge with widespread impact on quality of life, work capacity, and daily functioning.

The most commonly reported long COVID symptoms include persistent fatigue that does not improve with rest, cognitive difficulties often described as "brain fog" (problems with memory, concentration, and executive function), sleep disturbances, chronic pain in muscles and joints, exercise intolerance, shortness of breath, and headaches. Many patients experience multiple symptoms simultaneously, creating a complex clinical picture that can be difficult to address with any single intervention.

Researchers have proposed several mechanisms that may contribute to long COVID symptoms, including persistent microclots and microvascular damage, chronic inflammation, immune dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroinflammation. These proposed mechanisms share a common thread: impaired oxygen delivery and utilization at the tissue level. This is why researchers have turned their attention to hyperbaric oxygen therapy as a potential supportive approach.

Standard treatments for long COVID remain limited, and many patients seek complementary approaches to manage their symptoms. Wound Healing

Smoke Inhalation

Pets rescued from house fires may suffer from smoke inhalation, carbon monoxide exposure, and thermal airway damage. Research suggests that HBOT may help by rapidly displacing carbon monoxide from hemoglobin and delivering high concentrations of oxygen to compromised lung tissue. Veterinary emergency clinics have reported using HBOT as part of their smoke inhalation treatment protocols.

Neurological Conditions

Veterinary researchers are investigating the potential role of HBOT in supporting animals with neurological conditions, including intervertebral disc disease (IVDD), a common condition in certain dog breeds. Early case reports suggest that HBOT, used alongside standard veterinary treatments, may support neurological recovery in some patients.

Thermal Burns and Tissue Injury

Animals that have suffered burns or significant tissue trauma may benefit from increased oxygen delivery to support the healing process. Veterinary clinicians have explored the use of HBOT as an adjunct therapy for burn patients, noting that the increased oxygenation may help reduce secondary tissue damage and support faster recovery.

The Process

How Veterinary HBOT Works

Veterinary HBOT follows the same core principles as human hyperbaric oxygen therapy. The animal patient is placed inside a pressurized chamber where the atmospheric pressure is gradually increased, typically to between 1.3 and 2.0 ATA depending on the clinical protocol. At these elevated pressures, significantly more oxygen dissolves into the blood plasma, enabling oxygen to reach tissues with compromised circulation. This process is governed by Henry's Law, which states that the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional to the pressure of that gas above the liquid.

There are several important considerations specific to veterinary patients. Most animals are placed inside the chamber without a mask, as the entire chamber is pressurized with oxygen. Veterinary staff monitor patients through the chamber's transparent walls, watching for signs of stress, discomfort, or ear-related issues during pressurization. Many animals, particularly dogs, adapt well to the chamber environment after one or two sessions and remain calm throughout the treatment. Sedation is rarely necessary but may be used in cases where an animal is particularly anxious.

Treatment protocols vary based on the condition being addressed and the species of the patient. A veterinarian trained in HBOT will develop a customized protocol that specifies the pressure level, session duration, and total number of treatments. Sessions typically last between 45 and 90 minutes, with the pressurization and depressurization phases conducted gradually to minimize discomfort for the animal.

Between sessions, veterinary teams assess the patient's response to treatment and adjust the protocol as needed. The frequency of sessions depends on the condition: acute injuries such as snake bites may warrant daily or twice-daily sessions initially, while chronic conditions may involve a more gradual treatment schedule spread over several weeks.

How HBOT Accelerates Wound Healing

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) supports wound healing by delivering concentrated oxygen under pressure directly into blood plasma, increasing oxygen levels in damaged tissue. This increased oxygen promotes angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation), stimulates collagen production, and enhances white blood cell function to fight infection. Wound healing is among the 14 FDA-recognized indications for HBOT, and the therapy has been the subject of over 10,000 clinical studies.

Chronic wounds fail to heal because the damaged tissue lacks adequate blood supply and oxygen. Without oxygen, cells cannot produce the energy needed for repair, collagen cannot form properly, and immune cells cannot effectively combat bacteria. HBOT breaks this cycle by dissolving oxygen directly into plasma under pressure, allowing it to reach ischemic tissue that red blood cells cannot access through compromised blood vessels.

The scientific evidence for HBOT in wound care is substantial. Systematic reviews published in Diabetes Care have reported higher wound closure rates in patients receiving HBOT compared to standard care alone. A Cochrane Review concluded that HBOT may reduce the risk of major amputation in diabetic foot ulcer patients. These findings have contributed to HBOT being incorporated into advanced wound healing protocols at hospitals and wound care centers worldwide.

The Science

How Oxygen Heals Wounds at the Cellular Level

Angiogenesis

Research indicates HBOT stimulates the growth of new blood vessels (angiogenesis) in the wound bed. These new capillaries deliver oxygen and nutrients to tissue that was previously starved, supporting the vascular infrastructure necessary for wound closure.

Collagen Synthesis

Oxygen is a required substrate for collagen production. HBOT provides the oxygen that fibroblasts need to synthesize collagen, the structural protein essential for building new connective tissue and closing wounds.

Immune Enhancement

White blood cells require oxygen to produce the reactive oxygen species that kill bacteria. Research shows HBOT may enhance leukocyte bactericidal activity, supporting the body in clearing infection from chronic wound beds that resist standard antibiotic therapy.

Edema Reduction

Hyperbaric oxygen causes vasoconstriction that reduces edema and swelling around the wound while simultaneously increasing the amount of oxygen dissolved in plasma. This reduces tissue pressure and improves circulation to the wound.

Stem Cell Mobilization

A study published in the American Journal of Physiology (Thom et al., 2006) reported that HBOT significantly increased circulating stem/progenitor cells in human subjects. These stem cells may migrate to wound sites and differentiate into the cell types needed for tissue repair.

Growth Factor Release

Research indicates HBOT may stimulate the release of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other growth factors that coordinate the complex biological processes involved in wound repair and tissue regeneration.

Clinical Applications

Wound Types Treated with HBOT

Wound healing is one of the most well-established medical applications of hyperbaric oxygen therapy and is among the FDA-recognized indications. The following wound types have been studied extensively in the context of HBOT as part of a comprehensive wound care protocol.

Diabetic Foot and Lower Extremity Ulcers

One of the most common FDA-cleared indications for HBOT in wound care. Diabetic wounds suffer from reduced blood flow and impaired immune function. HBOT is used to increase tissue oxygenation and support white blood cell activity. Medicare covers HBOT for Wagner grade III or higher diabetic wounds that have not responded to 30 days of standard care.

Radiation Tissue Damage

Radiation therapy can cause delayed tissue damage (osteoradionecrosis and soft tissue radionecrosis) months or years after treatment. HBOT is used to promote new blood vessel growth in radiation-damaged tissue, supporting oxygen and nutrient delivery. This is one of the most evidence-supported FDA-cleared applications of HBOT, with protocols of 30 to 60 sessions studied in clinical settings.

Compromised Skin Grafts and Flaps

When skin grafts or surgical flaps show signs of compromise due to inadequate blood supply, HBOT may improve graft survival by increasing oxygen delivery to the transplanted tissue. Clinical experience suggests early intervention with HBOT may help support graft viability.

Chronic Non-Healing Wounds

Wounds that have not responded to at least 30 days of standard treatment may benefit from HBOT. By addressing the underlying oxygen deficit in the wound bed, HBOT may help support the healing process in wounds that have stalled in the inflammatory phase.

Crush Injuries and Compartment Syndrome

Severe crush injuries cause swelling that restricts blood flow and damages tissue. HBOT is used in these cases to help reduce edema through hyperoxic vasoconstriction while maintaining increased oxygen delivery, with the goal of preserving tissue viability.

Necrotizing Soft Tissue Infections

Aggressive infections that destroy soft tissue are among the FDA-cleared indications for HBOT. The therapy is used alongside surgical debridement and antibiotics as part of a comprehensive treatment approach, potentially supporting immune function through increased oxygenation.

HBOT for Wound Healing FAQ

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is FDA-recognized for several wound-related conditions. The FDA has identified 14 conditions for which HBOT is recognized, including diabetic lower extremity wounds, chronic refractory osteomyelitis, compromised skin grafts and flaps, crush injuries, and delayed radiation injury (soft tissue and bony necrosis). The Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society (UHMS) also maintains a list of approved indications. OxyHealth chambers are FDA-cleared (510(k)) medical devices, providing confidence that the equipment meets rigorous safety and efficacy standards.

The number of HBOT sessions required depends on the wound type, severity, and individual patient response. For diabetic foot ulcers, treatment protocols typically involve 20 to 40 sessions, each lasting 90 minutes at 2.0 to 2.4 ATA. Radiation tissue injury may require 30 to 60 sessions. Acute traumatic wounds and compromised grafts may respond within 10 to 20 sessions. Most wound care protocols schedule sessions once or twice daily, five days a week. Your wound care specialist will monitor progress and adjust the treatment plan based on healing response.

HBOT has been studied for a wide range of wound types, several of which are among the FDA-recognized indications for HBOT. These include diabetic foot and lower extremity ulcers, venous stasis ulcers, arterial insufficiency ulcers, pressure injuries (bedsores), surgical wound dehiscence, radiation-damaged tissue (osteoradionecrosis and soft tissue radionecrosis), compromised skin grafts and flaps, crush injuries with compartment syndrome, necrotizing soft tissue infections, and chronic refractory osteomyelitis. The therapy is often considered for wounds that have not responded to standard treatments over a period of 30 days or more.

Oxygen plays a critical role in nearly every phase of wound healing. At the cellular level, HBOT promotes angiogenesis, which is the formation of new blood vessels that deliver nutrients and oxygen to the wound bed. It stimulates fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis, essential for building new connective tissue. HBOT enhances white blood cell bactericidal activity, helping fight infection in the wound. It also reduces edema and inflammation by constricting blood vessels while simultaneously increasing oxygen delivery. Research in hyperbaric medicine indicates that HBOT can increase tissue oxygen levels significantly, creating an environment that supports every stage of healing from inflammation through remodeling.

Many insurance providers, including Medicare, cover HBOT for specific FDA-recognized wound conditions. Medicare covers HBOT for diabetic wounds of the lower extremities (Wagner grade III or higher) that have not improved after 30 days of standard wound care. Coverage typically requires documentation from a wound care physician and evidence that the wound has failed conventional therapy. Private insurance coverage varies by plan and provider but generally follows similar criteria. OxyHealth recommends working with your wound care facility and insurance provider to verify coverage. Some clinics also offer self-pay options for patients whose conditions are not covered.

Clinical outcomes for HBOT in wound healing are well-documented. A systematic review published in Diabetes Care found that HBOT significantly increased the rate of healed diabetic foot ulcers compared to standard care alone. Patients often observe reduced wound drainage and inflammation within the first 5 to 10 sessions. New tissue growth (granulation) typically becomes visible after 10 to 15 sessions. Complete wound closure depends on the wound type and severity, but many chronic wounds that failed to respond to months of standard treatment show meaningful improvement within a 30 to 40 session HBOT protocol. Post-radiation patients frequently report significant pain reduction and improved tissue quality.

Research supports the role of HBOT in reducing amputation rates among diabetic patients with non-healing lower extremity wounds. A Cochrane Review analysis concluded that HBOT significantly reduces the risk of major amputation in patients with diabetic foot ulcers. By promoting angiogenesis and tissue oxygenation in ischemic wound beds, HBOT helps restore the healing environment necessary for wound closure. The therapy is most effective when used as part of a comprehensive wound care program that includes debridement, offloading, infection management, and blood sugar control.

Yes, HBOT is considered safe for patients with diabetes when administered under appropriate medical supervision. The primary consideration is blood glucose management, as HBOT sessions can affect blood sugar levels. Patients should monitor their glucose before and after sessions and communicate with their care team about any adjustments to medications. Over decades of clinical use, HBOT has maintained an excellent safety profile for diabetic patients.
